title: Historical Market Events
head: name
line: From Tulip Mania to the AI investment cycle: what happened, how investors behaved and what it teaches.

items.name: Tulip Mania
items.overview: One of the earliest recorded speculative bubbles. In the Dutch Republic, rare tulip bulbs became highly valuable assets, with prices rising dramatically as speculation increased before collapsing.
items.whatHappened: Investors began buying tulips not because they wanted the flowers, but because they believed prices would continue rising. Eventually demand weakened, confidence disappeared, and prices collapsed.
lessons: An increasing price does not automatically mean increasing value.
When everyone is focused on making money, risk often increases.
Narratives can overpower fundamentals.

items.name: South Sea Bubble
items.overview: One of history's earliest major financial bubbles. The South Sea Company became the centre of extreme speculation in Britain.
context: Government-backed privileges and enormous promoted future potential
Belief that trade would expand massively
Belief that wealth creation was guaranteed
Belief that prices would continue rising
items.whatHappened: Shares increased dramatically. Eventually expectations exceeded reality, confidence collapsed, and investors suffered significant losses.
lessons: A strong story does not replace financial reality.
Even intelligent people can participate in irrational markets.

items.name: The Great Depression
items.overview: The most severe economic downturn of the modern era.
items.whatHappened: In October 1929, stock markets collapsed. Bank failures, unemployment, and economic contraction followed.
behaviour: Euphoria, leverage, and overconfidence before the crash
Panic, forced selling, and fear during it
lessons: Debt amplifies both gains and losses.
Risk often appears lowest before it becomes visible.
Liquidity matters.

items.name: Nifty Fifty
items.overview: A period where investors heavily favoured a group of high-quality growth companies.
items.context: Companies viewed as exceptional businesses, certain winners, and worth any price, spanning consumer brands, healthcare companies, and technology businesses.
items.whatHappened: Investors paid extremely high valuations. Eventually growth expectations disappointed, valuations compressed, and stock prices declined.
lessons: Great companies can still be poor investments at excessive prices.
Quality and valuation must be considered together.

items.name: Black Monday
items.overview: The largest one-day percentage decline in stock market history.
items.whatHappened: On 19 October 1987, markets experienced a dramatic single-day collapse.
lessons: Markets can fall faster than expected.
Short-term volatility does not equal permanent loss.
Preparation matters.

items.name: Dot-Com Bubble
items.overview: A technology-driven speculative bubble.
items.context: The internet created genuine innovation, but investors began assuming almost every internet company would become successful.
items.whatHappened: Technology valuations rose dramatically. Many companies had little revenue, had no profits, and relied on future expectations. The bubble collapsed in 2000.
lessons: A transformational technology does not guarantee successful investments.
Great ideas still require good businesses.

items.name: Global Financial Crisis
items.overview: A global financial crisis caused by excessive leverage and weaknesses in the financial system.
items.whatHappened: Housing problems spread through the financial system, leading to bank failures, market collapse, and a global recession.
lessons: Understand leverage.
Complexity can hide risk.
Strong companies can survive weak environments.

items.name: European Debt Crisis
items.overview: A sovereign debt crisis affecting several European countries.
items.whatHappened: Markets questioned the stability of certain economies.
lessons: Markets price uncertainty aggressively.
Macroeconomic events affect sentiment.

items.name: Covid Market Crash
items.overview: A sudden global market collapse caused by an unprecedented health crisis.
items.context: Markets moved from optimism to fear rapidly.
items.whatHappened: Between February and March 2020, markets experienced one of the fastest declines in history. Recovery followed quickly as governments and central banks responded.
lessons: Unexpected events are unavoidable.
Prepared investors can act during uncertainty.
Markets often recover before confidence returns.

items.name: Inflation and Interest Rate Cycle
items.overview: A period of high inflation following pandemic disruption and significant monetary policy changes.
items.whatHappened: Central banks increased interest rates to control inflation, leading to bond market declines, growth stock valuation pressure, and a changing investment environment.
lessons: Interest rates influence asset valuations.
Different businesses perform differently in different environments.
Investors must understand economic cycles.

items.name: Railway Mania
items.overview: One of Britain's earliest major speculative bubbles. Railways represented a genuine technological revolution, but investment enthusiasm became detached from reality.
items.whatHappened: Thousands of railway companies were promoted and investors rushed to participate. Many had weak business plans, unrealistic projections, or were created primarily to attract capital. Investment eventually slowed, expectations collapsed, and many investors suffered losses.
lessons: A genuine innovation can still create poor investments.
The best technology does not guarantee the best returns.
Valuation matters even during revolutionary change.

items.name: Panic of 1907
items.overview: A severe financial crisis that demonstrated the dangers of excessive leverage and weak financial systems.
items.whatHappened: A failed attempt to manipulate a stock price triggered wider panic, leading to bank runs, liquidity shortages, and market instability. Private intervention eventually stabilised markets.
lessons: Liquidity can disappear when confidence disappears.
Financial systems depend heavily on trust.
Risk is often hidden during good times.

items.name: The Great Inflation
items.overview: A prolonged period of high inflation that changed investor understanding of monetary policy.
items.whatHappened: Inflation remained elevated for years. Interest rates increased, bonds performed poorly, and equity valuations changed.
lessons: Macroeconomic environments change.
Different assets perform differently across cycles.
Investors must understand purchasing power.

items.name: Japan Asset Bubble
items.overview: One of the largest asset bubbles in modern history.
items.whatHappened: At the peak, Tokyo property values reached extreme levels and Japanese equities traded at extraordinary valuations. The bubble collapsed, leading to long economic stagnation, weak equity returns, and banking problems.
behaviour: Belief that exceptional growth would continue
lessons: No market is immune from bubbles.
A great economy does not automatically mean great investment returns.
Price matters.

items.name: Asian Financial Crisis
items.overview: A financial crisis affecting several Asian economies.
items.whatHappened: Investor confidence collapsed, currencies fell sharply, and businesses and banks faced severe stress.
lessons: Debt denominated in unstable currencies creates risk.
Growth does not eliminate financial fragility.

items.name: Global Technology Crash
items.overview: The collapse following the Dot-Com bubble.
items.context: After years of technology optimism, internet companies attracted huge investment and valuations reached extreme levels.
items.whatHappened: Many technology companies failed and the Nasdaq experienced a major decline.
behaviour: Assuming new technology changed old rules
lessons: Disruption creates winners and losers.
A good story requires good economics.
Future potential must be priced reasonably.

items.name: Commodity Supercycle
items.overview: A major rise in commodity prices driven by global demand.
items.whatHappened: Prices increased significantly across oil, metals, and agricultural commodities. Eventually demand slowed and prices corrected.
lessons: Commodity businesses are highly cyclical.
High prices create incentives for increased supply.

items.name: Cryptocurrency Bubble
items.overview: Periods of extreme speculation around digital assets.
items.context: Crypto introduced genuine innovation through blockchain technology, digital ownership, and decentralised systems, but speculation increased dramatically.
items.whatHappened: Prices surged rapidly as many assets were purchased based on momentum, social media excitement, and expectations of further price increases. Large declines followed.
lessons: Innovation and speculation can exist simultaneously.
A rising price is not proof of value.
Understand what you own.

items.name: Meme Stock Phenomenon
items.overview: A period where heavily shorted stocks experienced extraordinary price movements driven by online communities.
items.whatHappened: Certain stocks experienced extreme volatility, and prices became disconnected from traditional valuation measures.
lessons: Markets are influenced by human behaviour.
Price movement does not always equal fundamental improvement.
Risk management remains essential.

items.name: AI Investment Cycle
items.overview: A modern investment cycle driven by artificial intelligence development.
items.whatHappened: Investment flowed heavily into AI infrastructure, semiconductor companies, and software platforms.
behaviour: Confusing technology potential with investment returns
lessons: Major technological shifts create opportunities and speculation.
The winners are often difficult to identify early.
Great companies can still be poor investments at extreme prices.
